Expedia has confirmed that attackers got into its systems through a compromised third-party data platform provider, in an attack that also hit other companies. It confirmed the breach to travel publication Skift on Nov 12.
## The claims
A new Russian extortion group called n0n, which focuses on data theft rather than encryption, claims to have stolen a vast trove. Its claims include more than 830 million loyalty program records, 58 million traveler profiles, hundreds of millions of account and credential records, about 2.5 million credit card spending records tied to hashed email addresses, and source code.
Expedia hasn't confirmed any of these figures and says its investigation is ongoing. The numbers should be treated as unverified attacker claims.
## How they got in
Security firms Wiz and Sentra attribute the intrusion to a stolen vendor key from Qubole, a data platform provider. That key gave the attackers a trusted path into Expedia's big data platform. Qubole has also been linked to exposed cloud credentials at other companies in recent weeks.
## Expedia's response
Expedia says it contained the attack once it learned of it, brought in outside experts, and that its platforms remain safe for travelers and partners.
who: Expedia customers and loyalty program members, and travelers whose bookings passed through Expedia's platforms.
todo: Change your Expedia password if you reuse it anywhere else, turn on two-factor authentication, and watch for travel-themed phishing that mentions your bookings or points.

title: Maileva breach exposes names and addresses of 22 million people in France
dek: A La Poste subsidiary that sends payslips, letters and invoices for businesses says attackers stole data on 22 million recipients. Bank details weren't affected.
body:
Maileva, a La Poste subsidiary that sends documents such as payslips, registered letters and invoices on behalf of businesses, was breached in mid-September. La Poste confirmed the incident to AFP, and its scale was reported on Nov 15.
## Who is affected
The roughly 22 million affected people are mostly recipients of mail sent by Maileva's client companies. Most never had any direct relationship with Maileva. Clients named in reports include social housing providers, medical laboratories in the Inovie group and patients of Foch Hospital via a subcontractor. In that last case, a hacker reportedly read payment reminders that included invoice numbers, treatment dates and amounts owed.
## What was taken
Maileva says first names, last names and postal addresses were stolen and that bank details weren't compromised. The company hasn't explained how the attackers got in.
## Response
Maileva notified France's data protection authority, the CNIL, filed a criminal complaint and informed affected client companies. A judicial investigation is underway. It isn't clear whether those companies will notify their own tenants and patients.
The case is a reminder that your data can leak through vendors you've never heard of, and that scammers can use even basic details to make fake letters look convincing.
who: Around 22 million people in France who received documents sent through Maileva by their landlord, lab, hospital or employer.
todo: Be wary of unexpected letters, calls or messages that cite your name, address or medical bills. Don't pay invoices or share details without checking directly with the organization.

title: Apify confirms attackers accessed customer accounts and data
dek: The web scraping company says one compromised credential let an attacker reach internal systems and customer accounts, exposing data including 2FA recovery codes.
body:
Apify, a Czech web scraping and automation platform with about 91,000 customers, has confirmed that a cyberattack compromised internal systems and customer accounts, SecurityWeek reports.
## Timeline
The intrusion happened on Nov 9 and 10. Apify discovered it on Nov 11, cut off the attacker and confirmed the next day that customer data was exposed. The attacker started with a single compromised credential and used it to gather more credentials and reach related accounts.
## What was exposed
According to a notification a customer shared online, the data included names, email addresses, billing details, account activity, IP addresses, salted password hashes, 2FA recovery codes, phone numbers and authentication tokens tied to Google and GitHub sign-ins. Card data was limited to cardholder names, expiration dates and last four digits. Apify hasn't said how many accounts were affected.
## Response
Apify added monitoring, changed critical internal secrets and revoked some OAuth connections, including GitHub, though it found no sign those connections were the attack route. It has contacted affected customers and says the investigation continues.
Because 2FA recovery codes were exposed, affected users should do more than reset their password.
who: Apify customers, especially those who build Actors from private GitHub repositories or sign in with Google or GitHub.
todo: Reconnect GitHub integrations as Apify instructs, change your password, regenerate 2FA recovery codes and review connected apps. Watch for phishing that uses your Apify account details.

title: Japanese furniture giant Nitori says up to 37.6 million records may have leaked
dek: Nitori found an intruder in its network who may have had access since mid-October. Names, addresses, birth dates and order details may be exposed, but not passwords or cards.
body:
Nitori, Japan's largest furniture and home goods retailer, says up to 37.62 million personal information records may have leaked after an attacker got into a system on its network, BleepingComputer reports.
## Timeline
Nitori detected the intrusion on Nov 6 and blocked it. Its investigation suggests the attacker may have had access since mid-October. The company is still working to determine the cause, including whether ransomware was involved, and how many individual customers are affected.
## What may be exposed
- For individual members and buyers: membership numbers, names, email and postal addresses, phone numbers, birth dates and gender
- For corporate members: company names, addresses and contact details
- Order information from Nitori's online store and its shops on e-commerce marketplaces
Nitori says account passwords and credit card information weren't exposed.
## Response
The company says it fixed the vulnerabilities involved, strengthened monitoring and notified Japan's Personal Information Protection Commission and the police. It will contact affected customers by email or post, and stresses that it will never ask for passwords, card numbers or PINs by email or phone.
It is one of several large Japanese breaches this month, alongside Iris Ohyama.
who: Nitori members and online shoppers in Japan, including corporate account holders.
todo: Expect phishing that uses your name, address or order history. Don't share passwords, card numbers or PINs with anyone claiming to be Nitori, and check messages against Nitori's official site.

title: Operation Endgame takes down Gootloader, CastleRAT and StealC servers
dek: Police seized 235 servers and 257 domains tied to three malware families and recovered about 6.4 million stolen logins belonging to more than 40,000 victims.
body:
Police in Europe and the U.S. have hit three malware operations in the latest round of Operation Endgame, The Hacker News and SecurityWeek report. Across Gootloader, CastleRAT and StealC, authorities seized 235 servers and 257 domains. Germany's BKA says about 6.4 million stolen logins belonging to more than 40,000 victims were recovered. No arrests were announced.
## The targets
- Gootloader spreads through fake legal documents planted on hacked websites, often WordPress, that are pushed up in search results. It then downloads other malware, frequently ransomware. The U.S. Justice Department says it has infected at least 25,000 computers since 2018 and was used against at least 44 U.S. ransomware victims, with about $28.8 million in losses. Police also cleaned malware from hundreds of hacked sites.
- CastleRAT is a remote access trojan known since 2025. Police seized 120 servers and 39 domains.
- StealC is an infostealer whose operators had rebuilt after a June takedown, partly on the bulletproof host Virtualine, which was shut down in late October.
## Check your exposure
Dutch police run a Check your hack service where you can enter an email address to see whether it appears in the seized data. Police warn they never send emails with links, so messages claiming otherwise are scams.
who: People whose logins were stolen by these malware families, and owners of hacked WordPress sites used to spread Gootloader.
todo: Check your email address at the Dutch police Check your hack service. Change passwords and turn on MFA for important accounts. WordPress owners should rotate admin passwords, remove unknown accounts and update everything.

title: Operation TorNado nets 354 dark web arrests across 14 countries
dek: Europol and partner police arrested dark web drug vendors and buyers and seized tonnes of drugs, more than 200 guns and over €200 million in cash and crypto.
body:
Europol and police in 14 countries have arrested 354 dark web vendors and buyers in Operation TorNado, Help Net Security reports. The operation ran from May 2025 to October 2026.
## Arrests and seizures
The U.S. made the most arrests with 132, followed by the U.K. with 59, Hungary with 45 and Germany with 41. In the U.S., authorities seized more than 4.8 metric tonnes of drugs, 152 firearms and more than €150 million in cash and cryptocurrency. European seizures included 950 kg of drugs, 57 firearms, over a million prescription tablets and more than €60 million in cash and crypto.
## The marketplaces
Investigators focused on users of the Archetyp, Bohemia, Nemesis, Kingdom and Tor2Door markets, all of which are already offline. They also went after forums, single-vendor shops and encrypted messaging services. Europol coordinated the national cases, sent staff to support actions in Czechia and Slovenia, and used blockchain analysts to trace payments.
## Why it matters
Marketplace takedowns grab headlines, but operations like this one show police following up for months afterward, using seized data to identify the people who bought and sold there. It follows earlier sweeps including SpecTor in 2023 and RapTor in 2025.
who: Dark web marketplace vendors and buyers; for most readers this is a law enforcement update rather than a risk.
todo: No action needed for most people.

title: U.S. seizes $1.2 billion in crypto stolen in the record Binance hack
dek: The FBI and Justice Department say they seized or restrained more than $1.2 billion of the cryptocurrency that North Korea's TraderTraitor group stole from Binance last month.
body:
The FBI said on Nov 12 that U.S. authorities have seized more than $1.2 billion in cryptocurrency stolen from the exchange Binance in October. The Justice Department said it obtained court approval to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion of the funds that had been frozen.
## Background
The Binance theft, which totaled more than $6 billion, is the largest crypto heist on record. The FBI has attributed it to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking group. The U.S. government and private companies have together frozen more than $2.7 billion of the stolen money, according to Associated Press reporting carried by SecurityWeek.
## What happens next
The government will typically file a forfeiture claim, and a judge will decide who has a legitimate claim to the recovered funds.
## A busy day for North Korea cases
The same day, the FBI blamed North Korea for a separate scheme it calls FaceStealer, which used hijacked messaging accounts and deepfake video calls to steal about $400 million over 18 months. U.S. officials have repeatedly said North Korea uses cybertheft to fund its government, including its weapons programs.
Recovering more than a billion dollars is unusual. Most stolen crypto is laundered quickly through mixers and cross-chain swaps.
who: Binance and its users, and the wider crypto industry targeted by North Korean hackers.
todo: No action needed for most people. Crypto firms should review North Korean social engineering tactics, especially fake job interviews and meeting invites.

title: NGINX2Root: a decade-old HTTP/2 bug lets attackers run code on NGINX servers
dek: F5 patched five critical NGINX flaws, including an HTTP/2 bug present since 2015. Proof-of-concept exploits are public, though no attacks have been seen yet.
body:
F5 released fixes on Nov 18 for five critical NGINX vulnerabilities. The most serious, CVE-2026-123007 and nicknamed NGINX2Root, sits in NGINX's HTTP/2 code and has existed since version 1.9.5, released in 2015. An unauthenticated attacker who can reach an HTTP/2 port can run code with the privileges of the NGINX worker process.
## How bad is it
F5 says exploitation requires ASLR to be disabled or bypassed, but researchers at Wiz and Xint showed the bug can be used to defeat ASLR as well. Xint went further and paired it with a Linux kernel SCTP flaw to gain root, even from inside a Docker container. Rapid7 and Censys have published proof-of-concept code. Rapid7's version needs roughly 128 GB of HTTP/2 traffic, which limits it on slower links. Censys estimates about 9 million internet-facing services run an affected version with HTTP/2 on.
F5, Wiz and Rapid7 say they have not seen attacks so far.
## The other four flaws
- CVE-2026-123633: HTTP/2 with backend proxying when worker connections run low.
- CVE-2026-123634: proxied server names built from variables combined with SSI or mirror subrequests.
- CVE-2026-121810: affects servers with HTTP/3 enabled.
- CVE-2026-113425: affects NGINX used as a mail proxy.
## Fixed versions
NGINX Open Source 1.31.9 (mainline) and 1.30.7 (stable) fix all five. NGINX Plus is fixed in 37.3.0.1 and 37.0.8.1. A plain reload does not load the new binary, so restart NGINX fully or do a live binary upgrade. Linux distribution packages may lag behind, so check your distro's advisories.
## If you can't patch today
Turning off HTTP/2 blocks the two HTTP/2 bugs but not the other three. Disable HTTP/3 where it isn't needed, and limit mail proxy listeners to trusted networks.
who: Anyone running NGINX Open Source 1.9.5 through 1.31.8 or NGINX Plus, especially with HTTP/2 enabled.
todo: Upgrade to NGINX 1.31.9 or 1.30.7 (or the fixed NGINX Plus builds) and fully restart. Until then, disable HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 where possible and watch for worker crashes or core dumps.

title: Java4Shell: a Java Base64 bug puts Jira, Jenkins and Keycloak at risk of takeover
dek: Oracle and OpenJDK fixed a memory corruption flaw in Java's fast Base64 decoder. CISA urged immediate patching, and scanners are already probing for it.
body:
Oracle and the OpenJDK project have shipped fixes for CVE-2026-114938, a flaw researchers at Calif have named Java4Shell. CISA urged organizations to patch right away.
## What's wrong
The bug is in an optimized Base64 decoder in the HotSpot JVM that only runs on x86-64 processors with the AVX-512 VBMI instruction set. That includes Intel Ice Lake and newer server chips and AMD Zen 4 and newer. A malformed Base64 string can make the decoder write dozens of bytes past the end of its buffer. Calif says it turned this into unauthenticated remote code execution against Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate in their default setups. It is holding back its exploit code. Other labs have reproduced crashes and memory leaks but not code execution.
Affected builds include Java 17.0.6 and later, plus Java 21, 25 and 27. ARM64 systems and standard Java 8 and 11 are not affected.
## Is it being exploited?
As of Nov 18, CISA and Canada's Cyber Centre said they knew of no attacks. By Nov 19, GreyNoise, watchTowr and Cloudflare were reporting scanning and exploit attempts. GreyNoise logged more than 150 matching requests but no confirmed intrusions.
## Fixes
- Oracle Java SE 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 and 27.0.1.1.
- Amazon Corretto and Azul Zulu have patched builds.
- Red Hat was still preparing its fixes, and some other OpenJDK distributions had not yet listed fixed builds.
Apps that bundle their own Java runtime need an update from the vendor. Container images must be rebuilt.
## Workarounds
If you can't patch yet, researchers say starting Java with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics, or -XX:UseAVX=2 on x86 only, removes the vulnerable code path. Atlassian recommends disabling AVX-512 for its Data Center products until patches arrive.
who: Organizations running Java 17.0.6+ or Java 21/25/27 on modern Intel or AMD x86 servers, especially Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, Artifactory and PingFederate.
todo: Update Java to the November builds, restart services and rebuild images. If that isn't possible, add -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics and watch logs for bursts of Base64 decoder errors.

title: Attackers exploit a critical Apache Roller flaw that needs no login
dek: The Apache Software Foundation says a deserialization bug in Roller's XML-RPC endpoint is being actively exploited. Version 6.1.6 fixes it.
body:
The Apache Software Foundation has warned that attackers are exploiting CVE-2026-129448, a critical flaw in the Apache Roller blogging platform. The bug is rated 9.8 out of 10.
## The flaw
The problem is unsafe deserialization in Roller's XML-RPC endpoint. An attacker with no account can send crafted data to that endpoint and run code on the server. Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 are affected, and the fix is in 6.1.6.
The ASF warns that on older versions, switching off XML-RPC in the admin interface does not fully protect the server, so upgrading is the real fix.
## What we know about attacks
The ASF says the flaw is being actively exploited, but it has not shared who is behind the attacks or who has been targeted.
This is the second critical Roller bug in a few months. CVE-2026-82384, also rated 9.8, was patched in September, and its advisory listed only version 6.1.5 as affected.
The flaw was found by a researcher using the handle n0mi1k and reported by Matt Raible.
## Why it matters
Roller is less common than WordPress, but it still runs blogs and internal sites at some companies and universities. Old, rarely maintained installs are easy targets, and a code execution flaw on a web server can be a foothold into the wider network.
who: Anyone running Apache Roller 4.0.0 through 6.1.4.
todo: Upgrade to Roller 6.1.6 now. If you can't, block outside access to the XML-RPC endpoint at the firewall or proxy, and check the server for webshells or unexpected processes.

title: CISA warns hackers are exploiting a critical Puppet server flaw
dek: A deserialization bug in Puppet Enterprise and Puppet Core lets any machine with a signed agent certificate run code on the Puppet Server. CISA added it to KEV.
body:
CISA added CVE-2026-115731, a critical flaw in Perforce's Puppet configuration management software, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Nov 17, citing reports of active exploitation.
## The flaw
The bug, rated 9.4, is a deserialization issue in how the Puppet Server processes reports sent by agents. Any client holding a valid agent certificate signed by the Puppet CA can use it to run code as the Puppet Server's service account. That matters because the Puppet Server pushes configuration to every managed machine, so taking it over can give an attacker reach across a whole fleet.
Affected versions:
- Puppet Enterprise 2026.0.0 before 2026.0.1, 2025.0.0 before 2025.12.1, and 2023.8.0 before 2023.8.13.
- Puppet Core 9.0.0 before 9.1.3 and 8.x before 8.22.2.
Perforce released fixes on Nov 3. The open-source fork OpenVox is also affected and has fixed releases.
## A second bug
The same researcher, Alain Rödel of Neodyme, also reported CVE-2026-115732, rated 9.0, which lets an attacker get around authorization checks based on certificate names. Neodyme says AI helped find both bugs.
## Attacks
Details of the attacks have not been published. Federal civilian agencies must patch by Dec 1.
who: Organizations using Puppet Enterprise, Puppet Core or OpenVox to manage servers.
todo: Upgrade the Puppet Server to the fixed release for your branch. Review which agent certificates have been signed, revoke any you don't recognize, and check the server for unexpected processes or files.

title: Poisoned releases of Microsoft's Agent Framework on PyPI stole cloud credentials
dek: Two malicious versions of the agent-framework package, which gets about 190,000 downloads a month, harvested Azure, GitHub and other secrets for under an hour.
body:
Attackers published two malicious versions of agent-framework, Microsoft's Python package for building AI agents, to the PyPI registry on Nov 17. The versions, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, went up 33 minutes apart and have since been quarantined.
## What the malware did
Both versions planted a .pth file. Python runs these automatically every time it starts, so the code ran even if the package was never imported. It collected:
- Azure CLI tokens, Azure DevOps tokens and managed identity tokens.
- Cloud instance metadata.
- Credential files for npm, git and Docker, among others.
Version 1.26.2 also grabbed GitHub Actions OIDC tokens, which can be swapped for cloud access in CI pipelines. The stolen data was sent to a webhook.site address.
## Exposure window
The malicious versions were live for about 45 minutes, roughly 8:35 to 9:20 p.m. UTC on Nov 17. The package is downloaded about 190,000 times a month, and automated builds that fetch the latest version are the most likely victims.
It is not yet known how the attackers got permission to publish the package, and no one has been publicly blamed.
## Why it matters
AI agent tooling is a growing target for supply chain attacks because it usually runs with broad cloud access. A single bad install on a build server can expose credentials for production systems.
who: Developers and CI/CD pipelines that installed agent-framework 1.26.1 or 1.26.2 on Nov 17.
todo: Pin agent-framework to 1.26.0, search build logs and lockfiles for 1.26.1 or 1.26.2, and if found, rotate every cloud, GitHub, npm and Docker credential the affected machine could reach.

title: F5 warns of six critical BIG-IP flaws that can crash traffic in some setups
dek: Stack buffer overflows in BIG-IP's traffic engine can be triggered without logging in when certain iRules or APM policies are used. Only hotfixes are available.
body:
Alongside its NGINX fixes, F5 disclosed six critical vulnerabilities in the BIG-IP data plane on Nov 18. All six are stack-based buffer overflows in TMM, the engine that handles traffic, and all are rated 9.8.
## Who is exposed
An unauthenticated attacker can crash TMM and interrupt traffic until it restarts, and F5 says code execution may be possible in some cases. The management interface is not involved. Each flaw only applies to a specific configuration:
- CVE-2026-123637: APM per-request policies that use both the Client Information and Endpoint Security agents.
- CVE-2026-121805: iRules using PEM::subscriber.
- CVE-2026-120292: iRules using MR::message route with an HTTP profile.
- CVE-2026-120285: iRules using PSC::ip_address with an HTTP profile.
- CVE-2026-116953: iRules using GENERICMESSAGE::route.
- CVE-2026-120722: iRules using DNS::scrape.
Some also affect BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes and BIG-IP CNF.
## Fixes
There is no workaround. F5 has released engineering hotfixes, which it notes have not been through full quality testing. Customers already running a custom hotfix will need a new one from F5 support.
watchTowr researcher Sina Kheirkhah found four of the flaws and F5 found the other two. F5 says none have been exploited. The batch also included six lower-rated BIG-IP bugs, including an iControl SOAP flaw fixed in versions 21.1.0.3, 17.5.1.10 and 17.1.3.6.
who: BIG-IP, BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes and CNF customers whose virtual servers use the listed iRule commands or APM policy settings.
todo: Search your iRules for the listed commands and review APM per-request policies. If any match, apply F5's engineering hotfix and restrict iControl SOAP and REST to trusted networks.

title: Optimizely hack served card skimmers and crypto stealers on CNN, BBC and Zoom sites
dek: Attackers abused a flaw in Optimizely's signup flow to inject malicious code into 178 organizations' experiment scripts for most of a day on Nov 16.
body:
For most of Nov 16, visitors to some of the world's biggest websites were served malicious JavaScript through Optimizely, a popular website testing and experimentation service.
## What happened
Optimizely says an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in its Experimentation account signup flow. The attacker used it to add code to customers' project scripts, which were then delivered from Optimizely's own CDN with a valid certificate, so browsers trusted them.
Researcher Scott Helme and Report URI analyzed 1,611 Optimizely scripts and found 188 infected files belonging to 178 organizations. Sites that loaded the code included CNN, BBC, Zoom, GitLab, Salesforce, Fox News, KLM, Air France, Smartsheet and UNICEF USA. On the BBC, the first injected script appeared around 4:21 a.m. UTC. All infected files were clean by about 11 p.m. UTC.
## What the code did
- Swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses on pages for the attacker's own.
- Captured payment card details typed into a site's own form fields. Cards entered in hosted payment frames such as Stripe were not captured.
- Collected cookies, page URLs and screenshots.
- Fingerprinted iPhones and iPads and tried to load iOS exploit kits.
No device compromise has been confirmed. Wallets linked to the attack received about $7,000. Optimizely has not said how many visitors were exposed.
## Response
Optimizely closed the flaw, removed the code, revoked tokens and sessions, and notified affected customers. Salesforce disabled Optimizely scripts on its sites while it investigates. Report URI found that most affected sites had no Content Security Policy that would have stopped the script.
who: People who visited affected sites on Nov 16, and companies that load Optimizely Web Experimentation scripts.
todo: Visitors: update iOS, check crypto transfers and card statements from Nov 16. Site owners: review Optimizely project code, keep third-party scripts off payment and login pages, and use a strict Content Security Policy.

title: Russian spies used data stolen from one U.S. group to break into another
dek: Google says Cold Relic, also known as Star Blizzard, turned a staff directory stolen in a 2025 hack into a convincing impersonation campaign against a second U.S. organization.
body:
Google's Mandiant and Threat Intelligence Group have described how a Russia-linked espionage group reused stolen data to breach a second victim. Google tracks the group as Cold Relic. It is also known as COLDRIVER, Callisto and Star Blizzard, and the U.S. has tied it to Russia's FSB.
## The first break-in
In late 2025, the group got into a U.S. organization's cloud productivity suite through a Super Admin account. It connected through a residential proxy near the victim to look local, and used MFA push fatigue until someone approved a prompt. It then registered its own device and added passkeys and MFA backup codes so it could keep coming back, even after password resets.
Over several months it downloaded the company's cloud drive, exported employee lists and domain data, synced mailboxes to outside clients and tampered with logs and alerts.
## The second victim
After it was kicked out, the group used what it had stolen. Posing as employees of the first organization, it contacted staff at a second U.S. organization through a secure messaging app and sent phishing links that captured Microsoft Entra ID credentials. It registered a new MFA device on the victim's single sign-on and bulk-downloaded files.
Neither victim has been named.
## The lesson
The attack relied on trust between partner organizations, not on software flaws. A message that seems to come from a known contact at a partner organization carries more weight, and the group knew exactly whom to imitate.
who: Organizations that use Google Workspace or Microsoft Entra ID, especially those working with government, defense or policy groups.
todo: Use phishing-resistant MFA for admins, alert on new MFA devices and passkeys, and after any breach revoke all sessions, passkeys and backup codes. Verify unexpected messages from partners through a second channel.

title: Google finds hackers using an AI agent that turns patches into exploits on its own
dek: Google's threat intelligence team found an 'exploit_agent' framework that compared patched and unpatched code, wrote exploits and ran them without human help.
body:
Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) says that for the first time it has seen attackers use an AI framework to both find and exploit vulnerabilities with no human in the loop.
## What Google found
The framework, called exploit_agent, was sitting on an exposed staging server. It takes a web application before and after a security patch, compares the two to work out what was fixed, writes an exploit for the old bug and runs it against targets. The server also held data stolen from victims and scripts for follow-up steps such as reconnaissance and planting webshells.
GTIG says the evidence points to interest in French media and entertainment websites and the education sector. It did not name the group behind it.
## A wider trend
The report lists other AI attack frameworks seen in real intrusions:
- Cairn, used against the U.S. aerospace sector.
- PentAGI, used for reconnaissance and scanning in Asia.
- Artex, which GTIG calls the most widely used, mainly by Chinese-speaking groups.
GTIG also observed a Chinese group building its own automated attack framework, likely for spying, and state-backed groups from China, Iran and North Korea using AI models in their work. It expects less stealthy criminal groups to keep adopting these tools.
## Why it matters
The gap between a patch being published and attackers using it keeps shrinking. If software can read a fix and produce a working exploit, waiting weeks to patch internet-facing systems becomes much riskier.
who: Any organization running internet-facing web applications, especially those that patch on a monthly or slower cycle.
todo: Shorten patch windows for exposed systems, prioritize fixes for web apps you can't hide behind authentication, and invest in automated detection and response.

title: Last of five U.S. Scattered Spider defendants gets six years in prison
dek: Scottish national Tyler Buchanan was sentenced for his role in a phishing and SIM-swapping scheme that stole at least $11.6 million in cryptocurrency.
body:
A U.S. federal judge has sentenced Tyler Robert Buchanan, a 24-year-old from Dundee, Scotland, to six years in prison, the Justice Department said on Nov 18. He is the last of five defendants charged in the U.S. case against members of the Scattered Spider hacking group.
## The scheme
Prosecutors say that between September 2021 and April 2023 the group sent hundreds of phishing text messages to employees of telecom, tech, cloud communications, gaming and cryptocurrency companies. Stolen logins were funneled to a Telegram channel that Buchanan ran with an accomplice. The group used them to get into company systems and look for cryptocurrency accounts, and got around two-factor authentication by SIM-swapping victims' phone numbers.
The government now says at least $11.6 million in crypto was stolen, up from the $8 million cited when Buchanan pleaded guilty in April to conspiracy to commit wire fraud and aggravated identity theft. A restitution hearing is set for Dec 11.
## The other defendants
- Noah Michael Urban: 10 years.
- Ahmed Hossam Eldin Elbadawy and Evans Onyeaka Osiebo: 45 months each.
- Joel Martin Evans: two years.
Buchanan was arrested in Spain in May 2024 and has been in U.S. custody since April 2025. Separately, two other alleged members were sentenced in the UK earlier this year over the Transport for London attack.
who: Telecom, tech and crypto companies targeted by SMS phishing and SIM swapping.
todo: No action needed for most readers. Companies should move staff off SMS-based MFA and train employees to report login-page texts.

title: Flash chip attack cracks Windows Hello and BitLocker PINs in days, not years
dek: TU Berlin researchers reset or forged firmware TPM anti-guessing counters with physical access. AMD confirmed a flaw, and longer PINs are the best defense for now.
body:
Researchers at Technische Universität Berlin have shown how someone with physical access to a PC can get around the lockout that stops PIN guessing on firmware TPMs. That lockout is what protects Windows Hello and BitLocker PINs from brute force.
## How it works
Firmware TPMs keep their saved state, including the count of wrong guesses, on the PC's flash chip. The researchers opened machines and either restored an older copy of that state to wipe the counter, using a small board to block counter updates on AMD PCs, or used voltage glitching to pull a signing key out of Winbond RPMC flash chips and forge counter values.
In the lab, they found a four-digit Hello PIN on an AMD-based HP laptop in under an hour and a six-digit BitLocker PIN on a Framework laptop with an Intel chip in about seven minutes. Their worst-case estimate for a default six-digit BitLocker PIN is 20 days instead of 19 years.
## Vendor response
- AMD confirmed a firmware flaw, CVE-2026-43613, and plans fixes from November 2026 to February 2027.
- Intel said no Intel component was shown to be vulnerable. The Intel laptop fell through the Winbond chip.
- Microsoft rated the issue moderate and plans to raise its recommended minimum Hello PIN to six digits.
The Winbond weakness may need a new chip design to fix.
## What to do
This needs time alone with the device, so the main risk is lost or stolen laptops. Longer PINs blunt it quickly. Adding two digits multiplies the guessing time a hundredfold.
who: Owners of Windows laptops and desktops that rely on firmware TPMs, especially AMD systems and PCs with Winbond RPMC flash.
todo: Use Hello and BitLocker PINs of at least eight digits, or enhanced PINs with letters. Use TPM plus PIN for BitLocker, and install AMD firmware updates when your PC maker ships them.

title: European Commission confirms an AI-assisted cyberattack knocked staff systems offline
dek: The Commission says attackers used an AI tool in a late-October intrusion that disrupted HR, pay-related and translation services for more than 10 days. No group has been named.
body:
The European Commission has publicly confirmed that a cyberattack disrupted several of its internal services, and that the attackers used an AI tool to carry it out. A spokesperson said the incident is largely contained and the investigation continues.
## What happened
The intrusion was detected on October 22 and confirmed as an attack on October 26. The Commission took a number of applications offline as a precaution. Reporting by Politico and Euronews says the outage lasted more than 10 days and hit systems staff rely on every day:
- Sysper, the HR platform used for leave requests and payslips
- MyPMO, used for medical reimbursements
- Translation services, which went down on November 17
- JSIS, the staff health insurance portal, which a staff member said was still down on November 19
Tech Commissioner Henna Virkkunen briefed the College of Commissioners on November 18. Pay reportedly arrived on time.
## The AI angle
The spokesperson confirmed an AI tool was involved but did not name it. CERT-EU had warned in early November about ARTEX, an AI-driven penetration testing framework whose developer pulled it from public hosting after reports of misuse. Security Affairs says ARTEX is suspected, but that link has not been confirmed, and no threat group has been identified. The Commission said it knows of no ransom demand.
## Was data taken?
The official line is that there is no evidence of a breach of staff data, while Politico reported that large amounts of data may have been compromised. Under EU rules for its institutions, a confirmed personal data breach must be reported to the European Data Protection Supervisor within 72 hours. Staff have complained that internal communication about the outage was thin.
who: European Commission staff whose HR, reimbursement and insurance data sit in the affected systems, and other EU bodies sharing infrastructure.
todo: Commission staff should watch for official breach notices and be wary of phishing that references the outage. Organizations should treat AI-driven pentest frameworks as a real intrusion tool when tuning detections.

title: China-linked spies exploited a vCenter zero-day for two months before VMware patched it
dek: Broadcom fixed CVE-2026-123890, a 9.8-rated vCenter authentication bypass. Google says the Armory Castle group, formerly UNC5221, used it since early September.
body:
Broadcom has patched a critical authentication bypass in VMware vCenter, and Google says a suspected China-nexus espionage group was already exploiting it as a zero-day for more than two months.
## The flaw
CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS 9.8) sits in the VMware Directory Service. According to Google's analysis, an unauthenticated attacker who can reach the service over the network can leak an SRP session key and use it to obtain an administrator@vsphere.local session, giving full control of vCenter. Mandiant reported the bug to Broadcom, which shipped fixes on November 19 in advisory VMSA-2026-0009. The advisory itself does not mention exploitation.
## The attacks
Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant attribute the activity to Armory Castle, previously tracked as UNC5221. In the intrusions they investigated, the group first got in through a BeyondTrust Remote Support zero-day (CVE-2026-102764), moved to internal Linux appliances, then turned on vCenter. Its exploit tool, BONESAW, was used to:
- Pull the vCenter identity database and SAML signing material
- Create a rogue SSO administrator and forge SAML tokens to get past MFA
- Steal vCenter's master encryption key and database credentials, then reach ESXi hosts
The group also dropped web shells and backdoors, including one that uses Slack for command and control. BONESAW worked even on a vCenter already patched for an earlier bug, CVE-2026-59309, and Mandiant says it is effective against vCenter 7.x and 8.x.
## Fixed versions
Fixes are in vCenter 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200 and 8.0 U3m, plus Cloud Foundation 5.2.5. vCenter 7.0 has no public patch, as it is past end of general support.
## Hunting tips
Google points to scans of ports 9080, 5480 and 2012, SSH being switched on through the appliance management API, unexpected local admin accounts on vCenter, a listener on TCP 33992, and new SSH keys for root on ESXi hosts.
who: Any organization running VMware vCenter 7.x or 8.x, or vSphere/Cloud Foundation 9.x, especially if BeyondTrust Remote Support is also in use.
todo: Patch vCenter now, and move off vCenter 7.0. Then hunt for the indicators Google published, rotate SSO and SAML signing material if anything looks off, and check BeyondTrust appliances for compromise.

title: PHP patches seven critical flaws, including the phpAfterShell session bug
dek: PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28 and 8.5.13 fix seven critical memory and session bugs that can lead to code execution, a month after the PHP2Shell emergency releases.
body:
The PHP project has shipped another round of critical security releases, fixing seven flaws that it rates 9.2 under CVSS 4.0. Several could let a remote attacker crash a PHP worker or run code with its privileges. The fixes arrived on November 19, alongside the release of PHP 8.6.0, and come about a month after the emergency PHP2Shell patches of October 21. Those earlier releases do not include these fixes.
## What was fixed
- CVE-2026-115560, an input validation bug, fixed in all four supported branches
- CVE-2026-126714, a race in how session data is written, dubbed phpAfterShell
- CVE-2026-129289, a request smuggling-style issue affecting setups that keep FastCGI backend connections open, such as nginx with fastcgi_keep_conn
- Four use-after-free bugs: CVE-2026-129182, CVE-2026-129474, CVE-2026-129481 and CVE-2026-129496, some of which affect only newer branches
## phpAfterShell
Researchers at Depthfirst found that if a PHP worker is killed partway through writing a session file, for instance by an out-of-memory kill, attacker-supplied serialized data can be left behind and later loaded as objects. In the setup they tested, the upload progress feature writes to the session before any application code runs. Turning that into code execution still depends on a suitable gadget chain in the app. No attacks using it have been reported. The fixed releases also switch upload progress off by default, so apps that rely on it will need to turn it back on.
## What to do
Upgrade to PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28 or 8.5.13, or move to 8.6.0, and rebuild container images. Check the version actually serving traffic, since distributions often backport fixes without changing version numbers. If you cannot patch yet and do not need upload progress, set session.upload_progress.enabled to 0 and restart workers, though that is only a partial fix. PHP 8.1 and older are end-of-life.
who: Anyone running PHP 8.2 through 8.5, including WordPress, Drupal, Laravel and other PHP apps, plus container images and hosting platforms that bundle PHP.
todo: Upgrade to the fixed release for your branch, rebuild containers and restart PHP-FPM. As a stopgap, disable session upload progress, or move session storage to Redis or a database.

title: Ruby2Shell: a one-byte overflow in Ruby may expose default Rails apps
dek: Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14 fix seven memory bugs. Researchers say the worst, CVE-2026-132825, is reachable without login in default Rails and Sinatra apps.
body:
The Ruby core team has released Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14 to fix seven memory-safety bugs in the interpreter's regular expression engine and its string case conversion code. Three are rated critical, and the maintainers say proof-of-concept code shows some of them can be used to run code.
## Ruby2Shell
The one drawing the most attention is CVE-2026-132825, a one-byte heap overflow that happens when Ruby changes the case of text in single-byte encodings such as ISO-8859-1 or Windows-1252. Veria Labs, which named it Ruby2Shell, says the bug can be reached without authentication in default Rails applications and classic Sinatra apps, through the way Rack handles incoming requests. That claim comes from the researchers, not the Ruby maintainers. Veria says it will release its exploit about a week after disclosure, so the window to patch is short.
## The other bugs
- Two more critical issues: a double free when compiling certain character-class patterns, and a heap overflow when a compiled regex grows too large
- Three high-severity heap overflows and out-of-bounds reads, including one in Regexp#to_s
- A moderate out-of-bounds read that can leak memory or crash a process
Only Ruby2Shell has a CVE so far. The others are tracked by GitHub advisory IDs. Credit for four of the findings goes to Ada Logics and Anthropic. No attacks have been reported.
## Patch the interpreter, not just gems
Updating Rails or other gems does not help here. The fix is in Ruby itself, so app servers, background workers and container base images all need the new interpreter, followed by a restart or rebuild. Ruby 3.2 and earlier are end-of-life and will not get fixes. Teams should also look at code that builds regular expressions from user input.
who: Teams running Ruby 3.3, 3.4 or 4.0, especially internet-facing Rails and Sinatra apps, and anyone shipping Ruby in container images.
todo: Upgrade to Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 or 3.3.14, rebuild images and restart app servers and workers before the public exploit lands. Retire Ruby 3.2 and older.

title: Hackers break into clustered Cisco Expressway servers soon after a public exploit
dek: F6 says attackers used CVE-2026-76466, a 9.8-rated root command flaw, to breach a Russian organization's Expressway cluster. Cisco's advisory still lists no known abuse.
body:
Attackers have started exploiting a critical Cisco Expressway flaw shortly after proof-of-concept code was posted to GitHub, according to security firm F6.
## The flaw
CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS 9.8) lets an unauthenticated attacker run commands as root through the Expressway database service. It only affects Expressway Core and Expressway Edge, both virtual and appliance versions, when they run in a cluster. Cisco disclosed it on October 21 and fixed it in Expressway X15.5.20. There are no workarounds, and customers on X14 or older have to move to a fixed release.
## The attack
F6 investigated a breach at an unnamed Russian organization. The intruders first compromised two internet-facing Expressway devices running X15.5.3, then used the cluster connection to reach two internal nodes. From there they ran custom Python scripts to scan the network, try SMB, SQL Server and WinRM access, and search GitLab, all aimed at collecting credentials. F6 noticed the scripts were edited during the intrusion and contained comments typical of AI coding assistants. It did not tie the attack to any known group.
Cisco's advisory had not been updated at the time of reporting and still said the company was unaware of malicious use.
## What to do
- Upgrade clustered Expressway systems to X15.5.20
- If you cannot patch right away, F6 suggests blocking TCP ports 4371 and 4372 at the firewall for everything except trusted cluster nodes
- Review the Erlang system log on Expressway devices for signs of exploitation, and check F6's published IP addresses and file paths
Because Expressway often sits at the network edge for video and voice traffic, a compromise gives attackers a foothold that points straight into the internal network.
who: Organizations running clustered Cisco Expressway Core or Edge, physical or virtual, particularly where the devices face the internet.
todo: Upgrade to Expressway X15.5.20. Until then, restrict TCP 4371-4372 to cluster peers, and check Expressway logs and downstream systems for credential theft.

title: FastUnlock: an unpatched Windows trick runs programs from the lock screen
dek: A researcher released a lock screen bypass that uses Narrator to launch programs on a locked PC under a limited account. Microsoft has no fix yet.
body:
A researcher posting as Nightmare Eclipse has published FastUnlock, a technique that lets someone with physical access to a locked Windows PC start programs without signing in. Microsoft has not released a fix or an advisory, and no CVE has been assigned.
## How it works
The method abuses Narrator, the built-in screen reader, to move through the lock screen and reach an option that ends up launching a program. It requires a Microsoft account to be reachable through the lock screen's account recovery options. ThreatLocker tested the method the same day it was posted and confirmed it works.
The program runs under a limited account, which ThreatLocker identified as WSIAccount, rather than as an administrator or the logged-in user. That limits what an attacker can do directly, but it still provides a way to run code on a machine that its owner believes is locked.
## Why BitLocker does not help
Many organizations use BitLocker with automatic TPM unlock. In that setup the drive is already unlocked by the time the lock screen appears, so FastUnlock does not need to break encryption or recover the key. A BitLocker startup PIN protects a powered-off machine, but not one that is sitting at the lock screen.
## Is anyone using it?
There are no reports of FastUnlock being used in real attacks, and Microsoft has not published a list of affected versions. Until it does, any Windows machine that meets the conditions should be treated as possibly vulnerable.
who: Windows users and IT teams, especially those with laptops that travel or shared machines in public spaces.
todo: Don't rely on the lock screen alone. Shut down or hibernate laptops that leave your control, add a BitLocker startup PIN on sensitive devices, and tighten physical access until Microsoft ships a fix.

title: Drupal fixes a critical installer flaw that could let attackers reinstall sites
dek: CVE-2026-132165 lets an unauthenticated attacker abuse install.php to try to reinstall a Drupal site and take it over. A proof-of-concept exists, and fixes are out.
body:
Drupal has fixed a critical flaw in its core installer that could let an attacker with no account take over some sites. It is the second critical code execution bug in Drupal core in roughly two months, following a Field UI flaw patched in mid-October.
## The bug
CVE-2026-132165, covered in advisory SA-core-2026-017, lets an unauthenticated visitor use the built-in installer at /core/install.php to attempt to reinstall a site. Success can mean full site takeover or remote code execution. The Drupal Security Team scores it 18 out of 25 on its risk scale, but notes that the vulnerable configurations are uncommon and that exploitation is complex. Some attack paths fail if the web server cannot write to settings.php.
The bug was found by Anthropic's OSS Scanner, an automated opt-in service for open-source projects. The advisory records that a proof-of-concept exploit exists, though no attacks have been reported. Drupal had warned in advance that exploits could appear within hours or days of release.
## Affected and fixed versions
- Drupal 10 before 10.6.22
- Drupal 11.0.0 up to 11.3.22
- Drupal 11.4.0 up to 11.4.13
Fixed releases are 10.6.22, 11.3.22 and 11.4.13.
## A big end-of-life problem
Drupal's own figures show about 29% of reporting sites ran end-of-life branches in early November. Drupal 10 and 11.3 lose security coverage in December, and the project plans to shorten security support for minor versions from 12 to 8 months in 2027, citing the rising volume of AI-generated vulnerability reports.
## What to do
Update, and then block access to /core/install.php anyway, using a web server deny rule, an .htaccess rule or a Composer script that removes the file. A finished site has no need for its installer to be reachable.
who: Administrators of Drupal 10 and 11 sites, and agencies or hosts managing many Drupal installs.
todo: Upgrade to Drupal 10.6.22, 11.3.22 or 11.4.13, block public access to /core/install.php, and plan upgrades off branches that are losing support in December.

title: CISA flags four exploited flaws in Apache Axis, REDCap, LiteLLM and Synology NAS
dek: The new KEV entries are tied to Confluence intrusions, cryptomining, LLMjacking and ransomware on NAS devices. Federal deadlines for three of them fall on Nov 21.
body:
CISA added four actively exploited vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 18. Each is linked to a different kind of attack.
## Apache Axis and Confluence
CVE-2026-90436 (CVSS 9.8) is an unauthenticated code execution flaw in Apache Axis 1.x, an old SOAP library that is end-of-life and has no official release with a fix. Rapid7 saw it exploited against Atlassian Confluence Data Center, which uses Axis for its legacy remote API. After getting in, the attackers dug through the Confluence database and attachments for credentials and card numbers, tried AS-REP roasting against Active Directory, and used a stolen service account to sign in to Microsoft 365 about 12 hours after the first exploit attempt. Rapid7 linked the activity to the group exploiting N-able N-central servers to plant cryptominers.
## REDCap
CVE-2026-90817 (CVSS 9.8) is a code injection bug in REDCap, the research data platform common at universities and hospitals. It needs a valid public survey hash but no login. Safe Security saw an unknown actor use it to install a web shell and the XMRig miner, with cron jobs and SSH keys for persistence.
## LiteLLM
CVE-2026-40217 (CVSS 8.8) affects BerriAI's LiteLLM AI gateway. Google says attackers used it to turn limited inference keys into admin access, part of LLMjacking campaigns that hijack paid AI model access at organizations across several regions.
## Synology DSM
CVE-2024-10441 (CVSS 9.8) is a code execution flaw in Synology's NAS operating system that is being used to deploy C3RB3R ransomware on exposed devices.
## Deadlines
Federal civilian agencies must address the Synology, REDCap and Axis flaws by November 21 and LiteLLM by December 2.
who: Confluence Data Center admins with the remote API enabled, research institutions running REDCap, teams running LiteLLM gateways, and owners of internet-exposed Synology NAS devices.
todo: Patch REDCap, LiteLLM and Synology DSM using vendor advisories. Disable Confluence's XML-RPC/SOAP remote API or upgrade to Confluence 10, and remove or patch Axis 1.x elsewhere. Take NAS admin pages off the internet.

title: N-able says hackers breached a server behind Mail Assure and SpamExperts
dek: A days-long outage of N-able's hosted email security portals was caused by an intrusion, not a configuration problem. Credentials stored on the platform may have been exposed.
body:
N-able has confirmed that a disruption of its Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud services was caused by a cyberattack. The outage began on November 16, and the company first blamed a mix of platform configuration and service dependencies before saying on November 18 that a security incident was behind it.
## What was hit
N-able says unknown attackers got into a single web server used by the two email security services. In a statement to SecurityWeek, the company said the attackers may have accessed some credentials stored on the platform. It has found no evidence that customer data, including tenant mailboxes, was compromised.
The disruption affected both services in the Americas, Asia-Pacific and Europe. Mail flow and inbound and outbound filtering kept working, but the management portal, APIs, quarantine, logging and mailbox synchronization went offline. As of November 19, N-able said it was still validating and hardening the portal before turning access back on.
## How N-able responded
- Took the affected server offline
- Rotated internal platform credentials
- Revoked existing customer API tokens and invalidated OAuth tokens
- Reset passwords for local users
No threat actor has been named. N-able says this incident is separate from the N-central vulnerabilities that forced it to take N-central's cloud offline earlier this month, though it is a second serious security problem for the managed service provider software vendor in a matter of weeks.
who: MSPs and businesses that use N-able Mail Assure or SpamExperts Hosted Cloud for email filtering.
todo: Follow N-able's guidance for your setup, expect to recreate revoked API tokens and OAuth connections, change any local passwords, and review logs for unusual activity tied to platform credentials.

title: JPMorgan, Visa and Mastercard blame vendors after N0n leaks customer data
dek: The N0n extortion group posted data it says came from the three firms. Each says a third-party provider was hit and payment systems were not.
body:
JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard have each said a third-party provider suffered a security incident, after the N0n extortion group claimed on November 16 that it had stolen data about their customers. N0n marked all three as not having paid and offered the data for download on its leak site.
## What each company said
- JPMorgan said on November 19 that attackers accessed marketing data held by some of its vendors, possibly including customer names and email addresses. It said services were not disrupted, that the incident is unrelated to its banking outage earlier in the week, and that it will contact affected customers and offer free credit monitoring where appropriate.
- Visa said the data came from a third-party provider in Asia-Pacific and that its own systems and payment data such as card numbers were not affected.
- Mastercard said a provider exposed a limited set of email addresses and non-payment details for a small group of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefits program. Its network and cards are unaffected.
None of the companies named the vendors or gave a count of affected people.
## What is in the leak
Reuters reviewed the files and found more than 16,000 JPMorgan customer email addresses, some with phone numbers and postal codes, plus about 124 bank employee addresses. The Visa files held thousands of emails, phone numbers and marketing campaign records, mostly from Asia-Pacific markets.
## Who is N0n
N0n emerged in September 2026 and lists about 200 alleged victims. It is the same group that claimed data tied to Expedia through a vendor earlier this month, part of a pattern of hitting large brands through their marketing and data suppliers.
who: Customers of JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard, especially those enrolled in card benefit or marketing programs, who may get targeted phishing.
todo: Be suspicious of emails or calls that reference your bank or card and ask you to log in or confirm details. Go to the official app or website directly, and take up any credit monitoring offered.

title: Ukraine and the FBI detain ransomware suspects tied to $40.5 million in payments
dek: Police say the group posed as IT support on the phone to get into at least 28 companies, then stole data, encrypted systems and demanded crypto ransoms.
body:
Ukraine's National Police, working with the FBI, have detained four key members of a ransomware group that officials say collected more than $40.5 million from at least 28 companies. The investigation ran for more than two years.
## How the group operated
According to Ukrainian police, members phoned employees while posing as IT support and talked them into handing over login details or installing remote access software. One member kept the employee on the line while another broke into the network. Once inside, the group stole data, encrypted files and threatened to publish what it had taken unless the victim paid in cryptocurrency.
In one case described by police, the group took 1.4 TB of data from a U.S. company, demanded $10 million and received about $5 million, then moved on to other companies in the same corporate group. Victims included oil and gas, pharmaceutical, industrial, logistics, financial and infrastructure firms.
## The crackdown
- 66 searches in Kyiv and 11 regions, with U.S. law enforcement taking part
- Computers, phones, bank cards and about $370,000 plus 20,000 euros seized
- At least 27 members identified from Ukraine, Kazakhstan and Russia, within a wider network of more than 60 people across eight jurisdictions
Police say some members previously worked with the Conti ransomware operation. The suspects face charges including membership in a criminal organization and unauthorized interference with computer systems, which carry up to 15 years in prison. The ransom figure is an official estimate, and total damages are still being calculated.
## The lesson
The group's main tool was a phone call, not an exploit. Help desk impersonation remains one of the most effective ways into a company.
who: Companies in energy, pharma, manufacturing, logistics and finance, and any organization whose staff can be talked into installing remote access tools.
todo: Tell staff that IT will never cold-call asking for passwords or remote access installs, set up a callback procedure through a known number, and block unapproved remote access software.

title: Nvidia investigates after The Gentlemen ransomware gang lists it as a victim
dek: The Gentlemen added Nvidia to its leak site without details. Nvidia says a third-party partner may have been affected but it sees no sign its own systems were breached.
body:
The Gentlemen ransomware group has added Nvidia to its leak site, posting the company's logo and a short description and promising to release stolen information later. The listing gives no details about how or when an attack took place, and it does not by itself show that any Nvidia data was taken.
## Nvidia's response
A company spokesperson said Nvidia is investigating an incident that may have affected a third-party partner. So far it has found no sign that Nvidia's own systems or networks were affected, and it is monitoring the situation. Nvidia did not name the partner or say whether any Nvidia-related data was exposed.
## Who are The Gentlemen
The group appeared around mid-2025 and later opened an affiliate program, letting other criminals use its ransomware in exchange for a cut. Microsoft tracks it as Storm-2697. Its leak site now lists more than 1,100 alleged victims, mostly in manufacturing, healthcare, transportation and financial services. It uses double extortion: stealing data before encrypting systems, then threatening to leak it.
Sophos says Gentlemen affiliates typically get in with stolen credentials and then rely on legitimate admin tools, which makes them harder to spot. In one case Sophos investigated, ransomware was deployed less than a day after the first sign of hands-on activity.
## Why it matters
Leak site claims against big brands are often tied to suppliers rather than the brand itself, as Nvidia suggests here. Even so, data shared with partners can be just as sensitive, and the episode is a reminder to know what each vendor holds.
who: Nvidia partners and customers, and organizations in manufacturing, healthcare, transport and finance that The Gentlemen affiliates target most.
todo: No action is needed for Nvidia customers yet. Organizations should require MFA on remote access, watch for unusual use of admin tools, and review what data third parties hold.

title: Equinor fights off a cyberattack on its IT systems as production keeps running
dek: Norway's energy giant says an ongoing attack hit some IT systems, reportedly including internal email. Oil and gas output was not affected, and no attacker has been named.
body:
Equinor, the Norwegian energy company and Europe's largest gas supplier, said on November 17 that it had detected an ongoing cyberattack against some of its IT systems and had mobilized resources to stop it and restore its systems.
## What Equinor says
The company said oil and gas production is not affected. It described the incident as not being a virus attack, so there is no risk of it spreading, and said there is no indication that employees, partners or suppliers are affected or that data was stolen. Norwegian news agency NTB and a source cited by Reuters reported that internal IT applications were hit and the company's internal email system was down.
## Government reaction
Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) said it is aware of the attack and ready to help. A spokesperson said the risk facing Norwegian organizations is high. NSM raised the national cyber threat level to 4 out of 5 last month, warned that attacks could affect water and electricity supplies, and said successful attacks on Norwegian companies had tripled over the past six months.
## Who is behind it?
No group has claimed the attack and nobody has been publicly blamed. A pro-Russian DDoS campaign against Norwegian government websites in August has not been linked to this incident.
## Why it matters
Equinor's gas exports became central to Europe's energy supply after Russian pipeline flows dropped, which makes it an obvious target. Keeping IT problems away from production systems is exactly the separation energy companies are urged to maintain, and Equinor says that held this time.
who: Energy and critical infrastructure operators in Norway and across Europe, and Equinor's partners and suppliers.
todo: Energy firms should confirm IT and OT networks are properly separated, rehearse running operations without corporate email, and watch for phishing that uses the Equinor incident as a lure.

title: Amazon: China-linked operator's AI agents found a medical-imaging zero-day and took root on a university server
dek: Amazon says Cairn-driven AI agents found a path-traversal flaw in MONAI Label in about 11 minutes, then used it to get root. An exposed, passwordless control panel gave the operation away.
body:
Amazon Threat Intelligence says a suspected China-linked operator used autonomous AI agents to discover and exploit a previously unknown flaw in MONAI Label, an open-source server used to label medical images, and ended up with root access on a university server.
## How Amazon saw it
On September 10 Amazon found the operator's own Cairn control panel sitting on the internet with no password. Cairn is an open-source framework that runs AI agents as automated penetration testers. The panel exposed task settings, prompts and run history, which let Amazon reconstruct a roughly 48-hour campaign that began September 8 against universities in East Asia outside mainland China.
## What the agents did
Most attempts failed. The agents spent about 16 hours and 148 actions trying to break a Redis server at one university, and also tried Log4Shell, an SSRF against a Qdrant instance and password sprays against PostgreSQL, SSH and a GPU server.
Against MONAI Label they found a path-traversal bug in the upload code, where a file name supplied by the caller is used without checking it stays inside the storage folder. Amazon says the agents went from mapping the API to writing arbitrary files in about 11 minutes. Root came later, by planting a Python startup file and triggering a training job that loaded it. The operator then pointed the agents at a second university running the same software; Amazon believes it was compromised the same way but has not confirmed it.
## The flaw
- Tracked as CVE-2026-133968, rated 9.8.
- Affects MONAI Label 0.8.5 and earlier in the default setup, which has no login.
- A source fix was merged October 19, but at publication no fixed release was on PyPI.
## Attribution
Amazon links the operator to China with moderate confidence, citing Simplified Chinese prompts, China Standard Time settings and the choice of targets. No named group was given. This follows Unit 42's earlier report of a China-nexus operator using a Cairn fork.
who: Universities, hospitals and research groups running MONAI Label, and anyone exposing AI or research tooling to the internet without authentication.
todo: Take MONAI Label off untrusted networks, turn on authentication, run it under a low-privilege account, build from source with the October 19 fix, and look for unexpected Python startup files or unusual training jobs.

title: WhatsApp fixes three bugs, including one it believes a scammer abused
dek: An Android flaw in Click to WhatsApp ad replies could reveal a recipient's IP address. WhatsApp found it while disrupting a scam campaign. Two other bugs show no sign of abuse.
body:
WhatsApp has disclosed fixes for three vulnerabilities, one of which it says was probably used by a scammer.
## The bug tied to scams
CVE-2026-23871 affects WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business for Android before version 2.26.17.4. It comes from incomplete checks on external URLs in ad-reply messages used by Click to WhatsApp ads. A crafted message could pull media from an attacker-controlled server, which would reveal the recipient's IP address.
WhatsApp rates it low impact. Its own security team found it while disrupting a scam campaign, and the company says it believes a scammer used it to make scam messages look more credible. It did not say how widespread the activity was or whether any scams succeeded.
## Two medium-impact bugs
- CVE-2026-102769 is an SQL injection in WhatsApp for Android before 2.26.35.74. A malicious order-details message sent from an unofficial client could delete locally stored WhatsApp files and, through a delivery-receipt timing trick, leak a single bit about the chat database if the recipient was online. It was reported through Meta's bug bounty.
- CVE-2026-44908 sits in the code that verifies remote attestation for Meta AI's confidential computing backend. Someone already inside Meta's infrastructure could have used a certificate not signed by the chip maker's key to get past the hardware trust check. WhatsApp says such a certificate would have had to be published to a third-party transparency ledger first, and the ledger shows no abuse. Fixes landed across iOS, Android and Mac builds from version 2.26.23.x and 2.26.24.x.
## Why it matters
An IP leak sounds minor, but in a scam it can help an attacker tailor a lure to a victim's location or confirm a number is live. The fact that WhatsApp found the bug by watching scammers shows how small flaws get pulled into fraud.
who: WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business users on Android, iOS and Mac running older builds.
todo: Update WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business to the latest version from the official app store, and treat unexpected business or ad-reply messages with suspicion.

title: SBC Medical Group says hackers took data on more than 2 million clinic customers in Japan
dek: The Nasdaq-listed firm told the SEC that attackers breached a platform it runs for Japanese clinics, taking customer records, passwords and staff data. A separate incident hit a booking vendor.
body:
SBC Medical Group Holdings, a California-based company listed on Nasdaq that manages cosmetic and medical clinics in Japan, has disclosed a breach affecting more than 2 million people in a filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.
## What was taken
Attackers got into an online platform SBC manages and reached databases holding customer information for some of its clinics. According to the filing:
- Basic details for about 1.62 million people, including names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, dates of birth, gender, patient card numbers, member IDs and survey answers.
- Reservation request data for about 255,000 people and web inquiry form content for about 218,000.
- Treatment descriptions and image file names for about 4,500 people, and treatment names with review text for about 15,000.
- Customer passwords, plus card data for 14 people whose cards SBC says had expired or could not be used.
- About 20,000 employee records with names, IDs and passwords, and banking, pension and tax details for 459 staff.
## A second incident
Separately, attackers used administrator accounts at Tribeau, a third-party reservation service, to reach data on about 19,000 people, including names, phone numbers, ages and requested treatments.
## Response
SBC says it isolated the affected server, removed the intruders and reset passwords for all clinics it manages on Tribeau. It is still assessing the business impact. No attacker has been named and no ransomware claim has been reported.
## Why it matters
Cosmetic and medical treatment records are highly personal, which makes them useful for targeted extortion and phishing. Stolen passwords also put people at risk wherever they reused them.
who: Customers and staff of SBC-managed clinics in Japan, and users of the Tribeau booking service at those clinics.
todo: Affected customers should change any password reused from clinic accounts, watch for phishing that mentions treatments or bookings, and be wary of anyone threatening to expose medical details.

title: SonicWall tells Gen 6 firewall owners to replace them now: no more patches, even for critical bugs
dek: SonicWall says SonicOS 6.x devices are now a high-risk exposure and should come off the internet edge, pointing to faster, AI-assisted exploitation of unsupported gear.
body:
SonicWall is urging customers still running Generation 6 firewalls to retire them right away and stop exposing them on the internet edge. The company says these devices will no longer get security fixes, including for critical vulnerabilities, and that any Gen 6 unit still in service should be treated as a high-risk exposure.
## Which devices
The warning covers SonicOS 6.x hardware and virtual appliances, including the TZ300 through TZ600 series, SOHO and SOHO 250 models, the NSA 2600 to 6600 and NSa 2650 to 9650 lines, NSv virtual firewalls, SuperMassive 9200 to 9800 and NSsp 12400/12800. SonicWall's recommended replacement is a Gen 8 firewall running SonicOS 8.
## Why now
SonicWall points to attackers using AI to find and exploit flaws in unsupported edge devices faster. The Hacker News notes that Google Mandiant's M-Trends 2026 report puts the average time to exploit at negative seven days, meaning flaws are often exploited before a fix exists, and that Cisco Talos found nearly a quarter of 2025's CVEs hit network devices. SonicWall firewalls have been a repeated target for ransomware crews and other attackers.
## If you can't replace them yet
SonicWall lists interim steps:
- Turn off management over the WAN, including HTTPS, SSH and SNMP.
- Disable SSL VPN, or limit it to known source addresses.
- Require MFA on every remote-access and admin account and reset local passwords.
- Shut off unused services and interfaces.
- Watch logs for odd logins and configuration changes.
These reduce exposure but do not fix future bugs, so replacement should still be scheduled.
who: Organizations and small businesses still running SonicWall Gen 6 firewalls (SonicOS 6.x), especially ones used for remote access.
todo: Inventory Gen 6 units, replace internet-facing and VPN devices first, and until then disable WAN management, restrict or disable SSL VPN, enforce MFA and reset local passwords.

title: Linux KVM bug let a cloud VM read 127 GB of its AMD host's memory
dek: CVE-2026-99312 affects AMD hosts with nested virtualization on. Fixed upstream kernels are out, but several distros have not shipped them yet. Disabling nested virtualization is the stopgap.
body:
A flaw in the Linux kernel's KVM hypervisor lets a guest virtual machine read, and in some cases write, memory belonging to its host on AMD servers with nested virtualization enabled. It is tracked as CVE-2026-99312.
## What the researcher showed
Oren Yomtov of Terra Security found the bug and reported it through DigitalOcean's bug bounty. In a test on a DigitalOcean host he read about 127 GB of host RAM from inside a VM. On his own bare-metal server he also wrote 32 bytes into live host kernel memory. DigitalOcean confirmed the issue and rated it critical for its shared cloud.
## Root cause
A 2022 fix for an older bug, CVE-2022-3344, did not reset a nested page-table pointer when a virtual CPU is reinitialized. That leaves a pointer to freed memory. The faulty code dates to kernel 6.1 and was backported to 5.15.81 and 6.0.11. Intel hosts are not affected.
## Who can exploit it
An attacker needs root inside a VM running on a vulnerable host. Network access alone is not enough, but that is exactly the position any customer has on a shared cloud. There is no known exploitation outside the research and no public exploit code.
## Patch status
- KVM maintainers were told October 21 and merged a fix November 2.
- Fixed upstream kernels: 7.3.5, 6.18.64 and 6.12.118.
- At publication, Debian had a fix only in unstable, Ubuntu listed no fixed package, and Red Hat said EL9 and EL10 are affected with the fix deferred. EL8 is not affected.
- Scores differ: the kernel CNA rates it 8.8, while Red Hat treats it as denial of service and rates it 5.6.
The fix is in the host kernel and needs a reboot.
who: Cloud and hosting providers, and any organization running untrusted or multi-tenant VMs on AMD hosts with KVM nested virtualization enabled.
todo: Move hosts to a fixed kernel and reboot. Until then, check /sys/module/kvm_amd/parameters/nested and set 'options kvm_amd nested=0' if you don't need nested virtualization, then reboot.

title: New Bazuka Android malware hides its theft behind a fake picture of your home screen
dek: ThreatFabric found a modular Android framework with 23 modules for overlays, 2FA and SMS theft, remote control and crypto-address swapping, plus an AI-assisted panel for picking victims.
body:
Dutch mobile security firm ThreatFabric has disclosed Bazuka, a previously unknown Android malware framework built to manage large numbers of victims. It found the malware in late October while investigating an NFC-relay banking trojan.
## The trick
Bazuka's signature feature is an overlay that shows a screenshot of the phone's own home or lock screen. To the owner, the device looks idle, while the malware works underneath.
## What it can do
The framework has a dropper or downloader, a core component and 23 modules. Among them:
- Fake login overlays and keylogging.
- Capture of SMS messages and two-factor codes, and USSD-based call forwarding.
- Remote control of the device.
- A clipper that swaps cryptocurrency wallet addresses.
- Capture of the lock-screen PIN or pattern and interaction with NFC bank cards.
The core abuses accessibility services and wireless ADB debugging to grant itself permissions, switches off Google Play Protect, talks to its servers over two WebSocket channels and can delete itself.
## AI in the panel
The operator panel can connect to a local or API-based large language model to help score and choose victims. It can also create accounts for traffers, the people paid to drive victims to the malware, and build droppers with chosen permissions, which ThreatFabric suggests may help them get past store review.
## How it spreads
Droppers seen so far pose as a premium TikTok app. ThreatFabric has not tied Bazuka to a known group. The panel mixes English and Russian.
Bazuka arrives a week after Zimperium reported ArcticRAT, another Android RAT that uses LLMs.
who: Android users, especially those who sideload apps, and banks and crypto services whose customers use Android.
todo: Install apps only from Google Play, never 'premium' versions of popular apps from other sites, keep Play Protect on, and be suspicious of any app asking for accessibility access or wireless debugging.

title: ROMULUS ClickFix service pushes a remote-access trojan that can watch through your webcam
dek: Blackpoint Cyber says the ROMULUS delivery platform is spreading a RAT resembling CNCMachineRMS via fake MSI installers. Lures have even routed victims through ChatGPT custom GPTs.
body:
Researchers at Blackpoint Cyber say ROMULUS, a ClickFix-based malware delivery service, is distributing a previously undocumented remote-access trojan that closely resembles CNCMachineRMS.
## What ClickFix is
ClickFix attacks trick people into copying and running a command themselves, usually by showing a fake error, CAPTCHA or verification page that tells them to paste text into the Windows Run box or a terminal. Because the victim runs the command, it can slip past some security tools.
## The ROMULUS chain
Forescout first described ROMULUS last month as a service delivering CNCMachineRMS and the Legion Loader malware. In the sample Blackpoint studied, the victim's command uses PowerShell and msiexec to install a malicious MSI package. The installer poses as a Stardock utility and sideloads a malicious DLL that decodes and runs shellcode.
The resulting RAT supports remote desktop, live screen streaming, microphone and webcam capture, file management, system reconnaissance and running more payloads. It talks to its servers using DNS over HTTPS, which blends into normal encrypted web traffic.
ROMULUS lures have also used ChatGPT custom GPTs to send victims on to ClickFix pages.
## Part of a wider wave
