The report sits among a stream of ClickFix campaigns, including one using EtherHiding across more than 70,000 hacked websites, fake Zillow pages dropping NetSupport RAT and a fake Claude download page delivering the AMOS stealer to Mac users.
## Why it matters
ClickFix keeps working because it turns the user into the installer. Blocking the habit, not just the malware, is the defense.
who: Windows users and organizations whose staff can run PowerShell or the Run dialog, plus Mac users targeted by similar lures.
todo: Teach staff that no real website asks them to paste commands, restrict PowerShell and msiexec for ordinary users, and alert on msiexec launching from PowerShell or the Run box.

title: Icelandic web host 1984 shuts down websites, email and DNS after a major cyberattack
dek: The privacy-focused host took services offline on November 20, saying an attack that began the week before had escalated. CERT-IS is helping and no attacker has been identified.
body:
1984, an Icelandic web hosting company known for its focus on privacy and free speech, shut down its services on Friday, November 20, after what its managing director, Mörður Áslaugarson, described as a large and sophisticated cyberattack.
## Impact
The shutdown took down website hosting, email and DNS services that thousands of customers and businesses rely on. According to Áslaugarson, as reported by Icelandic broadcaster RÚV, the attack started the previous week and grew more intense before the company pulled the plug.
## Response
Iceland's national CERT, CERT-IS, and the Electronic Communications Office of Iceland are helping investigate. 1984 is restoring services in stages, starting with email and DNS, and says other services will come back once customer data and systems are judged safe. It has not given dates.
## What is not known
- Who is behind the attack. Investigators have not confirmed any group.
- Whether customer data was stolen.
- How the attackers got in, and whether ransomware was involved. No source has said it was.
Claims circulating about the attackers' identity and resources have not been independently confirmed.
## Why it matters
When a host goes down, every customer's site and inbox goes with it. Organizations that run DNS and email through a single provider have no fallback when that provider is hit. 1984 also hosts sites that value its privacy stance, which can make it a target in its own right.
who: Customers of 1984 in Iceland and abroad whose websites, email or DNS are hosted there.
todo: 1984 customers should prepare to rotate passwords and keys once services return, watch for phishing about the outage, and consider secondary DNS or email backup with another provider.

title: Oracle's November patch update fixes hundreds of flaws, including Java4Shell
dek: Oracle shipped 655 patches covering about 950 CVEs. Just over 300 can be exploited remotely without logging in, and 62 fix critical bugs. None are reported as exploited.
body:
Oracle released its November 2026 Critical Patch Update on November 17 with 655 new security patches across its product line. SecurityWeek counted 948 unique CVEs in the advisory, 640 of them listed in Oracle's product risk tables; the different totals come from how bundled third-party flaws are counted.
## The headline numbers
- Just over 300 patches fix flaws that can be exploited over the network without credentials.
- 62 patches address critical-severity bugs, including six rated at the maximum severity: five in Fusion Middleware and one in Analytics.
## Where the patches landed
- Hyperion: 267 patches, 107 of them for remote, unauthenticated bugs.
- Supply Chain: 74, with 36 remote and unauthenticated.
- Fusion Middleware: 71, with 53 remote and unauthenticated.
- E-Business Suite: 71, with 19 remote and unauthenticated.
- Communications: 31, with 21 remote and unauthenticated.
- Java SE: 11, all remotely exploitable without login.
- MySQL: 10 patches, plus fixes for Database Server, APEX, Enterprise Manager, REST Data Services and JD Edwards.
## Java4Shell
The Java SE update includes the fix for Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), the memory corruption bug in Java's Base64 handling that can lead to remote code execution. The Threat Desk covered it when it was disclosed on November 18.
## Exploitation
Oracle has not said any of these flaws are being exploited. That can change quickly. Oracle E-Business Suite and WebLogic have been prime targets for extortion groups, and attackers often reverse-engineer patches within days.
who: Organizations running Oracle Fusion Middleware, E-Business Suite, Hyperion, Database, MySQL, Java SE or other Oracle products.
todo: Review the November advisory, patch internet-facing Fusion Middleware, E-Business Suite and Java SE first, and keep Oracle admin interfaces off the public internet.

title: Rakuten Securities says data on up to 11 million accounts may have leaked from a test system
dek: Japan's large online broker found unauthorized access to a test environment holding real customer data. Rakuten Bank shares fell 19% the next day.
body:
Rakuten Securities, one of Japan's largest online brokerages, said on November 17 that an unauthorized party had accessed a system in its test environment, putting data from millions of customer accounts at risk.
## What may be exposed
- Login IDs and customer codes for up to 11.25 million accounts.
- Personal and financial details for up to 4.47 million accounts. Reported data types include names, addresses, birthdates, annual income and financial asset information.
The firm says login and trading passwords were not compromised. Reports differ on the exact date of the intrusion. No attacker has been named and no ransomware claim has been reported.
## Market reaction
Investors reacted sharply. Rakuten Bank shares fell 19% on November 18, the steepest intraday drop since it listed in 2023, and parent Rakuten Group fell as much as 7.5%.
## The test-data problem
A Bloomberg Intelligence analyst questioned why identifiable customer data was sitting in a test environment at all. Test and development systems often get weaker controls than production, yet they frequently hold copies of real data. That gap is a familiar route into breaches.
## Context
Japanese brokerages have been hit hard. In 2025 attackers took over thousands of trading accounts across several firms and used them to manipulate share prices. Recent weeks have brought leaks at SMBC Nikko Securities and Daiwa Securities Group, and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has announced an emergency cybersecurity package.
who: Rakuten Securities customers, and any company that copies production data into test or development systems.
todo: Rakuten customers should turn on every available login protection, watch for phishing posing as Rakuten, and review account activity. Companies should mask or synthesize data used in test environments.

title: Japan takes the Fugaku supercomputer offline after an intruder broke in through a status dashboard
dek: RIKEN says an attacker used Fugaku's public status page to reach internal servers and plant malware. Data on about 4,600 users, plus SSH and access keys, may be exposed.
body:
RIKEN, Japan's national research institute, has shut down Fugaku, one of the world's most powerful supercomputers, after a security breach. It turned the system off on November 14, disabled users' login keys and said it will only bring Fugaku back when it is safe to do so.
## How the intruder got in
RIKEN says that between November 10 and 13 an unauthorized party exploited the public web dashboard that shows Fugaku's operating status. From there the attacker reached several internal servers and planted malware aimed at user data. RIKEN has not yet said exactly what weakness was abused.
## What may be exposed
- Names, email addresses and user IDs of 4,222 Fugaku users.
- Names and email addresses of 375 users of Rikyu, a separate AI research system.
- SSH private keys and access keys stored on users' computers, and research data files.
The attacker used some of those keys to try to reach other systems. RIKEN says it has found no further unauthorized access and no theft of research results so far.
## Attribution
RIKEN has not attributed the attack.
## Recovery
RIKEN plans to fix the exploited weakness, rebuild compromised servers, review its network setup and add new monitoring. Fugaku, in shared use since 2021, supports drug discovery, weather forecasting and disease spread modeling, so the outage affects researchers across Japan.
## Why it matters
A public status page is easy to overlook, yet here it was the way in. Stolen SSH keys from research users can also open doors at other universities and labs where the same keys are trusted.
who: Fugaku and Rikyu users, and research institutions where those users hold accounts or reuse SSH keys.
todo: Fugaku users should revoke and replace any SSH or access keys used with the system, check other servers that trust those keys, and watch for emails impersonating RIKEN.

title: Alleged INC and Lynx ransomware affiliate extradited from Italy over attacks on U.S. hospitals and schools
dek: Kazakh national Roman Khlynovskiy appeared in court in Tennessee. Prosecutors say his '8-Digits Team' made $500 million in ransom demands and stole 70 million health records.
body:
Roman Khlynovskiy, a 43-year-old from Kazakhstan, has been extradited from Italy to the United States and made his first appearance in federal court in Knoxville, Tennessee, on November 16.
## The allegations
U.S. prosecutors say Khlynovskiy was part of the 8-Digits Team, a group that carried out attacks as an affiliate of the INC and Lynx ransomware operations. Its targets allegedly included hospitals, healthcare organizations, schools and companies in at least six states.
According to the reporting:
- The group's intrusions led to about $500 million in ransom demands.
- It claimed to have stolen 50 TB of data, including more than 70 million confidential health records.
- He faces charges including computer fraud, wire fraud, extortion, money laundering and identity theft, with a maximum of 27 years in prison.
These are charges, not convictions. Khlynovskiy has not been found guilty of anything.
FBI Director Kash Patel credited Italian law enforcement for the arrest and extradition. A Justice Department official described the case as one of the largest healthcare data breaches in decades.
## About INC and Lynx
The INC gang claimed a 2024 attack on McLaren Health Care in Michigan that disrupted systems and led to cancelled procedures, and has claimed attacks on Yamaha Motor, Xerox and the State Bar of Texas. Researchers at Unit 42 and Group-IB have found that INC either rebranded as Lynx or sold its code to Lynx operators.
## Why it matters
Affiliates do much of the hands-on hacking in ransomware schemes. Extraditions show that traveling outside safe havens carries real risk for them.
who: Healthcare providers and schools that INC, Lynx and similar ransomware affiliates target.
todo: Healthcare and education IT teams should review INC and Lynx indicators from CISA and vendor reports, enforce MFA on remote access, and keep offline backups of clinical systems.

title: Ghostscript bug turns print jobs, email attachments and upload forms into a way onto servers
dek: Researchers at pwn.ai show a font-loading flaw in Ghostscript can switch off its -dSAFER sandbox, and that files named .png or .pdf can reach it through common image libraries.
body:
Security firm pwn.ai has shown how a memory-safety bug in Ghostscript, the widely bundled PostScript and PDF interpreter, can be reached from the network even though it is rated as a local flaw. The bug, tracked as CVE-2026-125396 and scored 8.5 in a VulnCheck advisory, is a use-after-free in font loading. A crafted document can use it to turn off the checks that the -dSAFER sandbox normally enforces.
## How a local bug becomes remote
Many programs hand files to Ghostscript without users realizing it. Image libraries such as ImageMagick, Pillow and libvips, and a Qt plugin, pass content along even when the file carries a .png, .jpg or .pdf name. The researchers tested about ten applications and reached the bug, running as the low-privilege rendering account, in several ways:
- An anonymous print job sent to a shared print queue on Debian 13.
- An email attachment opened in Roundcube webmail.
- Public upload forms in the WordPress plugins Forminator and Essential Addons for Elementor, with no login.
- WordPress core itself, by a user allowed to upload files (Author and above by default).
## Fixes
Ghostscript 10.08.0, released on September 8, fixes the bug. WordPress 7.0.4 closed its own path under a separate CVE, and both updates are needed. Several Linux distributions still had fixes pending or in progress when the research was published. The public proof of concept shows only the memory technique, not a working shell, and fails on 10.08.0. There are no reports of attacks so far.
## Why it matters
Ghostscript often hides inside containers and bundled applications, where a normal operating system update does not reach it. Teams that process untrusted documents may be running an old copy without knowing it.
who: Anyone running print servers, webmail, CMS upload forms or image-processing pipelines that may call Ghostscript, including inside containers.
todo: Upgrade Ghostscript to 10.08.0 or later wherever it actually renders, including bundled and container copies; update WordPress to 7.0.4; require authentication on print queues; limit which file types image processors accept; and confine renderers with AppArmor or similar.

title: Planted AI prompts reveal months of data theft at inference providers; OpenRouter drops three
dek: Dragos seeded about 2 million prompts with canary links and keys. Some were stolen from providers' systems, AWS keys were tested within hours, and requests flagged for zero retention leaked too.
body:
Researchers at Dragos spent July to November seeding roughly 2 million prompts, sent through AI routing services, with trackable links and fake credentials. When those canaries were opened or used, they showed that prompts sent to several AI inference providers had been stolen, in some cases for months.
## What the canaries showed
- Attackers were inside three inference providers, the earliest from mid-July.
- In one case a few hundred planted AWS keys were taken in late October. Every request in those windows was captured, including some rejected before a model ran.
- Some stolen keys were tried within hours. The attacker listed storage buckets, searched secrets stores and tried to create new access keys and users.
- Some marketplace sellers switched on request logging and collected prompts themselves.
- Requests flagged for zero data retention were among those exposed, which shows such flags may only govern the first hop.
## The response
OpenRouter says it removed three providers, pulled 125 endpoints from zero-retention eligibility until they are validated again, and notified affected customers. It says its own systems were not breached. It has not named the providers it dropped.
Some providers have published their own accounts. Phala says an attacker controlled one of its inference servers until November 8. Together AI says prompt samples were downloaded after an AI coding agent committed a credential to a public GitHub repository.
## Why it matters
Businesses often paste secrets, customer data and source code into AI tools. When those requests pass through resellers and routers, every hop is another place they can be read, whatever the privacy settings say.
who: Companies and developers that send sensitive data or credentials to AI models through routers, resellers or third-party inference providers.
todo: Keep secrets out of prompts, choose upstream providers yourself or go direct to a first-party provider, check that privacy settings actually change routing, rotate any keys that may have appeared in prompts, and seed canary tokens to catch leaks.

title: GnuPG warns of a critical GPGME flaw that a booby-trapped OpenPGP key can trigger
dek: A double free in GPGME, the library many mail clients, XMPP apps, Samba and Gpg4win use for encryption, may allow code execution. GPGME 2.3.1 and Gpg4win 5.1.2 fix it.
body:
The GnuPG project has warned about a critical flaw in GPGME, the library that many programs use to talk to GnuPG for encryption and signatures. The bug, CVE-2026-129975, was found by researcher Johan Carlsson and reported through GitLab.
## The flaw
It is a double free in two functions that parse GnuPG's output. A malicious OpenPGP key with an extremely long user ID can trigger it. GnuPG says remote code execution cannot be ruled out. Its example attack sends signed data to an application, but it has not said which programs reach the bug without a user importing a key by hand.
Affected are all GPGME versions before 2.3.0, whether used as a shared library, a Windows DLL or statically linked into an application. That covers most mail clients that support OpenPGP, many XMPP chat clients, Samba, Gpg4win and GnuPG's desktop products. No attacks have been reported.
## Fixes
- GPGME 2.3.1 fixes the bug. Version 2.3.0 was never released publicly.
- Gpg4win 5.1.2 fixes it on Windows.
- A legacy 1.24.4 release is available for systems that cannot move to 2.3.1, without a promise of future patches.
The project says there is no workaround short of patching. Disclosure was originally planned for November 25 but was moved earlier.
## Why it matters
Because GPGME is often bundled or statically linked, updating the system library is not enough. Applications that ship their own copy need new builds from their developers.
who: Linux distributions, developers of mail and XMPP clients that support OpenPGP, Samba administrators and Windows users of Gpg4win.
todo: Update to GPGME 2.3.1 (or 1.24.4 on legacy systems) or Gpg4win 5.1.2, and check with vendors of applications that bundle or statically link GPGME for rebuilt releases.

title: One malicious webpage could make Meta's Muse AI agent leak its owner's chats and memories
dek: NebuSec says a page the agent visited could send conversation history and stored memories to an attacker without any prompt. A chained attack took over the agent's cloud computer.
body:
Researchers at NebuSec say they found a way to hijack Muse, Meta's personal AI agent, using nothing more than a webpage the agent opens while doing a task. Muse launched in September. It acts through the user's connected accounts, can make purchases and runs on its own cloud computer, with a monitoring layer called Sentinel meant to approve anything it sends out.
## What the researchers found
- A malicious page could make Muse send the user's conversation history and stored memories to an outside server, and change them, without asking the user.
- The same weakness could reach stored credentials for accounts connected to the agent.
- By chaining a flaw in Muse's built-in browser with a Linux kernel bug, they gained full control of the user's cloud machine. That exposed the credential store, saved files and Sentinel itself. They did not reach the shared server underneath or other users' machines.
## Status
NebuSec says the issue was fixed before it published its research. Meta had not commented, and it is not known whether anyone abused the flaw before the fix. No CVE has been assigned. This was a lab demonstration, and there are no reports of attacks.
## Why it matters
AI agents that browse the web on a user's behalf will read attacker-controlled content as a matter of course. When the same agent holds logins, payment access and long-term memory, a single poisoned page can be worth far more to an attacker than a normal phishing link.
who: Muse users, and any organization rolling out AI agents that browse the web while holding account credentials.
todo: Connect only the accounts an agent truly needs, avoid giving agents payment or admin access, review what they have stored in memory, and watch connected accounts for unexpected activity.

title: Signal now blocks screenshots by default to keep phone AI agents out of chats
dek: The messenger extends a Windows Recall defense to iOS and Android, calls AI agents built into operating systems an existential threat, and admits the protection is incomplete.
body:
Signal has started restricting screenshots of its app by default on Android and iOS. The goal is to stop AI assistants built into phone operating systems from reading users' chats off the screen.
## What changed
The protection applies to the agent features in iOS 27, and to Android versions where Signal can detect an AI assistant reading the screen. It extends a setting Signal added on Windows 11 in May 2025 after Microsoft unveiled Recall, which takes regular snapshots of the screen.
Signal Foundation president Meredith Whittaker has described agentic operating system features as an existential threat to Signal. The company also says screenshot blocking does not stop other ways agents could reach app data, such as files already stored on the device.
Users can turn the setting off under Settings, Privacy, App Security. Signal warns that doing so may expose their own and their contacts' messages to AI agents.
## What Signal wants from Apple and Google
- A documented way for apps to opt out of all AI data access, including screen reading, files, notifications and system APIs.
- Clearer documentation of how built-in agents access and process data.
The move comes days after Reuters reported that Meta's Muse agent reached Signal messages by using screen-capture and accessibility tools on a Mac and notification access on Android, rather than Signal's official connector.
## Why it matters
End-to-end encryption protects messages in transit, not on a screen that an AI agent can read. As phone makers build agents into the operating system, private messaging apps are pushing for a way to keep them out.
who: Signal users on phones with built-in AI assistants, and organizations that rely on Signal for sensitive conversations.
todo: Update Signal and leave screen security on; review iOS Excluded Apps and Android or Gemini connected-app settings to limit which apps AI assistants can read.

title: Attackers exploited an Entra Connect Health flaw to read Microsoft 365 tenant details
dek: Microsoft says the bug exposed admin email addresses, tenant IDs and license details, but no passwords or tokens. It was introduced in July and fixed server-side on November 19.
body:
Microsoft has told customers that attackers exploited a flaw in the Entra Connect Health service to get read-only access to information about their Microsoft 365 and Entra tenants.
## What was exposed
According to Microsoft's notice, the exposed data included:
- Email addresses of administrators and technical contacts.
- Tenant IDs, display names, initial domains and country or region.
- License tier and directory sync status, including the last sync time.
- Connect Health onboarding status, and an expired certificate from a service retired in late 2024.
Microsoft says no passwords, password hashes, tokens, valid keys, on-premises network details or Azure subscription data were exposed. The flaw could also have allowed changes to monitoring settings, but the company says it found none.
## Timeline
The bug was introduced on July 23 and discovered on November 9. Microsoft deployed a server-side fix on November 19 and notified affected customers on November 20. It has not said who carried out the attacks or how many organizations were hit. More than a dozen administrators posted notices online, and some managed service providers received notices for several tenants.
## Why it matters
The data is not enough to log in, but it gives attackers a ready-made list of who runs each tenant. That is useful for targeted phishing aimed at the people with the most access.
who: Organizations using Microsoft Entra and Entra Connect Health, and managed service providers that run multiple tenants.
todo: No patch is needed, but warn exposed admins about targeted phishing, require phishing-resistant MFA on privileged accounts, review Connect Health settings and Entra sign-in and audit logs, and check any notice in the Microsoft 365 admin center.

title: FBI investigates a breach of NCIC, the national database police check at every traffic stop
dek: People briefed on the probe say intruders reached the National Crime Information Center. How they got in, what they saw and who they are remain unknown, and the FBI has not commented.
body:
The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of the National Crime Information Center, the database that local, state and federal police across the U.S. use every day, according to CNN and the Associated Press, citing people familiar with the investigation.
## What NCIC holds
NCIC contains records on wanted and missing people, arrest warrants, stolen vehicles and guns, protection orders and other criminal-justice data. Officers query it during traffic stops, investigations and background checks.
## What is known so far
- The intrusion was discovered in recent days, but when it began is unclear.
- It is not known how the attackers got in, what data they viewed or took, or whether police access was affected.
- No group has been named, and there is no known link to ShinyHunters, which claimed an earlier breach of a platform tied to the FBI's jobs site.
- The FBI declined to comment. President Trump called the breach "not good" and said there was no known link to recent government technology outages.
The report follows other federal incidents this month, including a breach at the Department of Agriculture that forced payment systems offline.
## Why it matters
NCIC is one of the most sensitive databases in U.S. law enforcement. Access to it could expose informants, ongoing investigations and protection orders, or let someone check whether they are wanted. Even read-only access would be a serious intelligence prize.
who: Police and criminal-justice agencies that use NCIC, and people whose records it holds.
todo: Agencies should watch for FBI and CJIS advisories, review NCIC access accounts and audit logs, and enforce MFA on any system that connects to criminal-justice networks.

title: USDA security incident knocks farmer payment and loan systems offline
dek: After its security team found an intrusion, USDA reset database passwords across all environments, taking payment tools, loan portals and some staff VPN access down for days.
body:
The U.S. Department of Agriculture is dealing with a security incident that has knocked many of its applications offline, including systems used to send payments to farmers, Nextgov/FCW reported.
## What happened
USDA's Cybersecurity and Privacy Operations Center found the incident. To contain it, the department's IT staff reset database passwords across all environments. That forced every application relying on those databases to be reset too, and many went down over several days. Affected services included:
- Financial tools that handle payments between USDA and farmers.
- Customer portals that show the status of loans and aid and send notifications.
- Some staff VPN access.
An internal email from an acting assistant CIO at the Farm Production and Conservation Business Center described the incident, and a technical bulletin warned of intermittent outages throughout the week. Staff told reporters they had not been kept informed.
## What is unknown
USDA has not said who was behind the intrusion, how they got in or whether any data was taken. USDA and CISA did not respond to requests for comment.
## Why it matters
Farmers depend on USDA payments and loans, so outages can delay money they are waiting on. A department-wide password reset also suggests investigators could not rule out that database credentials were exposed.
who: Farmers, ranchers and lenders waiting on USDA payments, loans or aid, and federal IT and security teams.
todo: Expect delays in USDA payment and loan portals, be wary of phishing emails or calls that use the outage as a lure, and contact USDA offices through known phone numbers rather than links in messages.
